1:
Zophar the Naamathite rises as the third and last of the friends to speak, and the witnesses read his opening less as argument than as the boiling-over of a temper. The latin-fathers Gregory the Great frames the whole contest as a wrestling-match: as a mighty wrestler goes down into the arena and opponent after opponent presents himself, so against blessed Job first Eliphaz, then Bildad, and finally Zophar puts himself forward; yet their words never reach the height of that well-fenced breast, but are dealt, as it were, upon the air. It is the mark of the impertinent, Gregory adds, ever to answer by the opposite of what is rightly said — which is why Zophar begins with insult.

The other witnesses sketch the man. The reformed John Gill takes him for the youngest, since his turn is to speak last, and finds in him less modesty and prudence and more fire and heat than his fellows, the more irritated because Job had not receded from his sentiments under the others. The wesleyan-arminian voices press the harshness: John Wesley marvels how hard it is to keep calm in the heat of disputation — Eliphaz had begun modestly at ch. 4:2, Bildad a little rougher at ch. 8:2, but Zophar falls upon Job without mercy; and Adam Clarke calls him the most inveterate of the accusers, one who in "sour godliness" excelled all the rest and was "too crooked to speak much in measured verse."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry laments what intemperate passions even wise and good men are betrayed into by disputation, and reads the speech as a study in misrepresentation: Zophar would have Job thought idle and impertinent, a man that loved to hear himself talk, and gives him the lie and calls him a mocker, that it might seem a piece of justice to chastise him. Those minded to fall foul upon their brethren, Henry notes, find it necessary to put the worst colours upon them. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott completes the portrait by contrast: where Eliphaz was the poet and spiritual man and Bildad the man of tradition and authority, Zophar is the man of worldly wisdom and common sense, in some respects the most offensive of the three — astonished that Job has not been silenced by the others, he thinks he can do no less than help to silence him, and drags the argument down to his own level. The voices do not divide; together they set the tone for a speech that opens, alone among the three, not with a preface but with a charge.
2:
The speech breaks out at once in scorn, and the witnesses gather around the contempt packed into its opening question. The reformed John Gill hears Zophar insinuate that Job is a mere babbler, a talkative man who has words but no matter, saying much while there is nothing in what he says; whether he thought to bear down all before him by the sheer flood of speech or not, Zophar will not be deterred from answering. Gill records Bar Tzemach's turn of the phrase — "should not a man of a multitude of words be answered?" — a verbose man who deals in nothing but words, deserving a reply only to expose his emptiness and pull down his pride and vanity.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the impassioned couplet, "Shall the torrent of words remain unanswered, and shall the prater be in the right?" They pause over the very name of the speaker, which, explained from the Arabic, signifies "the yellow one," while the place he comes from means "pleasantness"; and they fix the Hebrew idiom, that the "multitude of words" (rob debarim) shall not go without its answer (responsum non feret), the verb carrying not the sense of being humbled but of being answered, as a suppliant is answered. The very impatience of the opening, they note, betrays the man: he counts himself bound to reply, as though Job's not being silenced by the other two were an affront that only he could remedy.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses sharpen both the taunt and the reply. Adam Clarke would render the first clause "to multiply words profiteth nothing," and fastens with relish on the phrase behind "a man full of talk" — literally "a man of lips" (ish sephathayim), a fit appellation for a great talker whose lips are the only active parts of his frame. John Wesley, however, quietly turns the question against the questioner: truly, sometimes the multitude of words should not be answered, for "silence is the best confutation of impertinence, and puts the greatest contempt upon it." Henry had already caught the same double edge, that whether or not such talk be answered, it should never be answered by pride and passion, but only, if at all, by reason and grace. So the witnesses agree that Zophar means to reduce Job to a mere "man of lips," even as they note that his own remedy — a flood of words to drown a flood of words — is the very fault he charges.
3:
"Should thy lies make men hold their peace? and when thou mockest, shall no man make thee ashamed?" — the harshest stroke yet, and the witnesses weigh both what the charge means and whether it was deserved. The reformed John Gill distinguishes two senses of the "lies" Zophar imputes: either lies in the common sort, untruths wilfully told, a scandalous thing which good men dare not commit; or doctrinal lies, errors in judgment, falsehoods concerning God and the things of God, which are not of the truth but against it. In either case, Gill allows, men ought not to sit by as deaf and dumb; truth must be contended for, and David would not suffer a liar to dwell in his house. Yet the whole weight of the verse turns on whether the case was rightly named.

Here the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke breaks in with a protest on Job's behalf. This, he says, "is a very severe reproof, and not justified by the occasion." Zophar could never truly think that the solemn and awful manner in which Job had spoken deserved to be called mere bubbling or empty noise, the force of the word rendered "mockest"; he might reckon Job's speech sarcastic and severe, but he could not honestly reckon it nonsense. John Wesley fills in the substance of the alleged lies and mockery: the "lies" are Job's assertions concerning his own innocency and concerning the counsels and ways of God, and the "mocking" is aimed at the friends' own counsels, which Job had met with such scorn as at ch. 6:14 and following.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the injustice of it into a rule of charity. Zophar represents Job as a man that made no conscience of what he said — a liar hoping by the impudence of lies to silence his adversaries, a mocker who bantered all mankind and was not ashamed to impose upon everyone that talked with him. But Job, Henry insists, "was not mad, but spoke the words of truth and soberness," and was thus misrepresented. We ought to put the best construction on the words and actions of our brethren that they will bear; it is the temptation of contenders to put the worst. The witnesses do not divide over the fact that some falsehood, if it were there, would warrant reproof; they divide, gently, over Zophar's reading of the man, Clarke and Henry alike judging that he has painted a sober sufferer in the colours of a shameless liar.
4:
Zophar now quotes Job back to himself — "for thou hast said, My doctrine is pure, and I am clean in thine eyes" — and the witnesses examine whether Job ever said any such thing. The reformed John Gill takes the verse as brought forward to support the charge of lying, resting on words Job had used in the foregoing chapters. But the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses the Hebrew and finds Zophar begging the question: the word rendered "doctrine" (likchi) is rather "my assumptions," what a man takes as right and true; and Job had not in fact said that his doctrine and life were pure and himself clean in God's eyes. He had only vindicated himself against their charge of secret sin and hypocrisy and appealed to God for his uprightness — so that Zophar, wanting something to answer, puts into his mouth a boast he never made.

John Wesley agrees and draws the distinction exactly: by "doctrine" Job had spoken concerning God and his providence, and by "clean" he had meant innocent before God, not that he had never sinned in act or expression; "Zophar perverts Job's words, for he did not deny that he was a sinner, but only that he was a hypocrite." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott weighs to whom the phrase "clean in thine eyes" is addressed — to God, to mortal men, or to Job himself — and prefers the first, since Job had at least hypothetically spoken of himself as righteous before God at ch. 10:15. Zophar, professing a superior wisdom, therefore wishes that God would show Job how far he falls short of it, and would credit him with part of the penalty still due to his sin.

Henry, tracing the whole indictment, lands on the same injustice. Job had indeed said, "Thou knowest that I am not wicked," at ch. 10:7, but he had also owned, "I have sinned," and never pretended to a spotless perfection; to infer from his denial of hypocrisy that he would not own himself a sinner "was an unfair insinuation." The witnesses do not divide over the doctrine but over the honesty of the report: whether the phrase points at Job's standing before God or before men, all of them — Clarke, Wesley, Ellicott, Henry — agree that Zophar has fastened on Job a claim to sinlessness that the sufferer never advanced, and made it the hinge of his attack.
5:
From misquoting Job, Zophar turns to invoke a higher voice against him — "but O that God would speak, and open his lips against thee" — and the witnesses hear in the wish a mixture of zeal and cruelty. The reformed John Gill reads it as Zophar's despair of doing the work himself: what the friends had spoken seemed to have had no effect upon Job, and so he entreats that God would take him in hand, stop his full mouth, convict him of his lies, refute his doctrine, and show him his folly in thinking himself pure and even free from sin in the sight of God. Only God, Zophar implies, can bring this stubborn man to a true sense of himself.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses recoil at the temper of the prayer. Adam Clarke exclaims over it in a single line: "How little feeling, humanity, and charity is there in this prayer!" — that a friend at a sufferer's side should long for God to appear not to comfort but to condemn. John Wesley reads the wish as, in effect, "let God plead with thee according to thy desire; he would soon put thee to silence"; and he draws the warning that we are commonly ready, with great assurance, to interest God in our quarrels, though "they are not always in the right who are most forward to appeal to his judgment, and prejudge it against their antagonists."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry seizes the same over-confidence and turns it into the finest irony of the chapter. So sure is Zophar of his cause that nothing will serve but that God must immediately appear to silence and condemn Job: "O that God would speak! for he would certainly open his lips against thee." Yet, Henry observes, "when God did speak, he opened his lips for Job against his three friends" — the very appeal Zophar makes so boldly would, when the LORD at last answered out of the whirlwind, fall out flatly against himself and his fellows, as the divine verdict of ch. 42:7 would show. We ought indeed, Henry grants, to leave all controversies to the judgment of God, which is according to truth; but those are not always in the right who are quickest to prejudge that judgment for themselves. The witnesses do not divide: they agree that Zophar's wish, meant as a thunderbolt against Job, was aimed, all unknowing, at the wrong man.
6:
Zophar's desired revelation is that God would "show thee the secrets of wisdom, that they are double to that which is," and add that God "exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth"; the witnesses find in the middle clause one of the real textual knots of the chapter. The reformed John Gill takes the "secrets of wisdom" as the deep things of God, mysteries which the creature cannot come at unless God reveal them — the manner of the Trinity, of the two natures in Christ, of the resurrection — things shown only by the Lord. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the same clause as the arcana imperii, the state-secrets of heaven: "God's way is in the sea," clouds and darkness are round about him, and what we know of him is nothing to what we cannot know; God, some add, knows a great deal more evil of us than we do of ourselves.

Over the phrase "double to that which is" the schools frankly disagree. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott is blunt: "this translation conveys no sense, and is not a translation." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke labours the disputed word (tushiyah), which means substance or essence and is rendered a dozen ways; Coverdale and the Vulgate give "how manifold his law is," the Septuagint "double to what it is with thee," and Clarke himself supposes Zophar to be comparing the wisdom revealed with the wisdom yet hidden, the perfection of the divine nature being manifold beyond the revelation already made. Keil and Delitzsch reject the common renderings of the neighbouring terms — cheqer is not "comprehension," nor tachlith "perfection" — insisting the words point to the very nature that underlies the visible.

On the sting in the tail all agree. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley takes "double" as simply "manifold," the secret wisdom of God being infinitely greater than what is revealed, so that Job does rashly to judge God's dealings he cannot fathom, and rashly to judge himself innocent because he cannot see his own sins, "whereas the all-knowing God sees innumerable sins in thee." And the closing verdict — that God "exacteth less than thine iniquity deserveth" — Henry turns into a hard mercy: whatever punishment is inflicted on us in this world is less than our sins deserve, so that instead of complaining of our troubles we should be thankful we are out of hell, as Lam. 3:39 and Ps. 103:10 both teach. The witnesses divide honestly over the words and unite over the doctrine: God's wisdom is unsearchable, and his hand, even in affliction, is lighter than justice would allow.
7:
"Canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection?" — and the witnesses take Zophar's twin questions as the high point of his speech, where for once he speaks nothing but truth. The reformed John Gill draws the careful line the verse draws: that there is a God may indeed be found out by searching the book of nature, for the creatures proclaim a maker; but what God is, his nature, being, and perfections, is past finding out. He recalls the old philosopher who, asked by a king what God was, kept begging another day and yet another, confessing that the more he considered the question the more obscure it grew; the wiser part of the heathen world knew there was a God, yet reared altars to the Unknown.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the incomprehensibility of God the ground of all submission. We that are so little acquainted with the divine nature are incompetent judges of the divine providence; we cannot find God out, how then dare we find fault with him? We may, by searching, find something of God, as Acts 17:27 allows, but we cannot find him out to perfection; we may apprehend him but cannot comprehend him, may know that he is but not fully what he is — "the eye can see the ocean, but not see over it." His wisdom cannot be fathomed nor his power bounded, and such knowledge is too wonderful for us, as Eccl. 3:11 confesses.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke answers Zophar's question with a rush of adjectives: what is God but a Being self-existent, eternal, infinite, immense, incomprehensible by mind or time or space? Who then can fathom his depths, ascend to his heights, or comprehend the infinitude of his perfections? John Wesley reads "find out" narrowly as to discover all the depths of his wisdom and the reasons of his actions, which is the point pressed against Job. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the literal force of the first clause — "canst thou attain to the searching out of God?" — the question being not whether God can be sought but whether the search can ever reach its end. The witnesses do not divide; they gather to one confession, that the finite creature may truly seek and truly find, yet never sound the bottom of the God he finds, and that this is reason enough to be humble and silent under a hand whose counsels lie beyond us.
8:
The dimensions of that unsearchable wisdom now open out — "it is as high as heaven; what canst thou do? deeper than hell; what canst thou know?" — and the witnesses divide chiefly over what the "it" is that so overtops us. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the antecedent on the divine wisdom, the Chokma of the verse above; its absoluteness, they say, is described by four dimensions, exactly as the apostle measures the love of God by breadth and length and depth and height in Eph. 3:18. The feminine form of expression, they note, keeps the wisdom in view, and they weigh the vexed spelling of the word for "measure" in the following line before settling their reading.

The reformed John Gill allows the same subject but offers an alternative that lifts the eye higher still: the words may be read "it is higher than the heavens," of the wisdom of God by which the heavens were made, or else, with the Vulgate, "he that is God is higher than the heavens" — for heaven is but his throne, the heaven of heavens cannot contain him, and he fills the infinite space beyond. How then is it possible to find him out, or to comprehend him? The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott keeps to the plainer construction and renders the pair of clauses simply, "the heights of heaven; what canst thou do? it is deeper than the grave; what canst thou know?"

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the four measures as instances drawn from the immensity of created things — high as the heavens, deep below sheol the invisible world, long beyond the earth and broad beyond the sea — all of them out of the reach of human power and knowledge; and if these things are so, how incomprehensible must he be who designed, created, preserves, and governs the whole. He crowns the thought with Milton's line, "These are thy glorious works, Parent of good! Almighty! thine this universal frame: how wondrous fair! thyself how wondrous then!" The witnesses do not finally divide over the sense of the verse, only over its reach: whether the height and depth belong to the wisdom of God, to God himself, or to the vast creation that is the nearest hint we have of either. All agree that the four dimensions are named not to inform us but to overwhelm us, and to shut the mouth that would call God to account.
9:
The measuring continues, and the last two dimensions are laid down: "the measure thereof is longer than the earth, and broader than the sea." The reformed John Gill notes how aptly length is ascribed to the earth and breadth to the sea, the ends of the earth standing for great distance and the sea being called the great and wide sea; but God and his perfections admit no such dimensions, for his wisdom, like his love, has a height that cannot be reached and a depth that cannot be fathomed, a length and breadth simply immeasurable. From this, Gill draws, it plainly appears that God is omniscient, omnipresent, and incomprehensible; and since this God is to be found in Christ, and in him only, it is in vain to seek him elsewhere.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the thought forward into the verses that follow, reading the measureless wisdom as the ground of the sovereignty about to be described. They render the sequel — "if he cut off, and shut up, or gather together, then who can hinder him?" — and explain that God is here conceived as one who manifests himself by passing to and fro in the powers of nature; should he meet a guilty man and arrest him and bring him to judgment, who then shall turn him back? The very verb for that summons, they observe, recalls the ancient form of public trial, in which the sentence was carried out before the assembled people.

So the two witnesses at this verse move together from the greatness of God's wisdom to the reach of his power. Gill lets the four dimensions preach humility and drive the seeker to Christ, in whom alone the hidden God is found; Keil and Delitzsch let them open into the next movement of the speech, where the immeasurable One becomes the irresistible One, the God whose passing through the world none can arrest and whose court none can defy. Neither strains the imagery beyond its plain force: the earth's length and the sea's breadth are set down not as boundaries that contain the divine wisdom but as the largest things men know, named only to be exceeded. The verse thus stands as the hinge of Zophar's argument, turning from the unsearchable to the unstoppable, and preparing the charge that a creature so far outmeasured has no standing to contend with his Maker.
10:
From the greatness of God, Zophar turns to his sovereignty — "if he cut off, and shut up, or gather together, then who can hinder him?" — and the witnesses attend to both the three verbs and the shadow they cast over Job's own losses. The reformed John Gill runs through the senses of the first verb: if God cut off the power and authority of the wicked, or the spirits of princes, or whole families, as he had cut off Job's; or, as others render it, "if he change," making revolutions in governments and in the estates of men; or "if he pass through" a land in judgment, as through Egypt — in every case there is none that can hinder him. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears the verse turned pointedly on the sufferer: unlimited and almighty, God will do whatever he pleases; and perhaps Zophar means Job's very case, "if he cut off, as he has done, thy children; if he shut up, as he has done, thyself by this sore disease" — who then can hinder the Sovereign disposing of his own?

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott shows how tightly the verse is woven from Job's own words. The verb "cut off" is the same used of the spirit that "passed before me" at ch. 4:15 and of God who "passeth on" at ch. 9:11; and the closing question borrows Job's own "who can hinder him?" from ch. 9:12. Some, Ellicott allows, understand the three terms forensically — if he arrest, and imprison, and hold assize — but he judges it likelier that Zophar is throwing Job's own statements back at him.

John Wesley glosses the verbs to the same effect — cut off a person or family, shut up in a prison or an enemy's hand, gather or scatter a household — and reads "hinder" as "contradict him, or charge him with injustice in such proceedings." The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the whole to its height: if he that made all out of nothing think fit to reduce all to nothing, if he shut up in the net of affliction as at Ps. 66:11, who can arrest the sentence or oppose the execution, control his power or arraign his wisdom? The witnesses do not divide over the sovereignty; they differ only over the register of the verbs — whether forensic arrest, cosmic change, or the plain undoing of a man's house — and Clarke and Ellicott alike feel how the general truth is being sharpened into a private wound.
11:
Zophar grounds God's right to judge in his perfect knowledge — "for he knoweth vain men: he seeth wickedness also; will he not then consider it?" — and the witnesses part, quietly, over that final clause. The reformed John Gill reads the opening as "men of vanity," which all men are, lighter than vanity itself; and the Lord knows them all, the vanity of their minds, the vain thoughts within them, their idle words and empty lives — so that it is no wonder he does as he pleases with them. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the phrase as "men of falsehood," and presses that God sees both what is in man and what man does, and cannot be an indifferent spectator of either.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the verse as a portrait of the all-seeing Judge. God observes vain men — every man at his best estate being altogether vanity — and knows the projects and hopes of the vain, so that he can blast and defeat them, and sits in heaven and laughs at them. He observes bad men too: all the wickedness of the wicked, however secretly committed or artfully disguised, is naked and open before the all-seeing eye of God, who sees it not to approve it, as Hab. 1:13 declares, but to animadvert upon it. "Will he not then consider it? Yes, certainly he will, and will reckon for it, though for a time he seem to keep silence."

Over just that clause the grammatical-historical witnesses set a different accent. Charles Ellicott renders it "though he regardeth it not," that is, God seems not to see the wickedness he in truth perceives — the very appearance of divine inattention that so tries the sufferer. John Wesley, on the other side, keeps the sense of active judgment: God knows man exactly, perceives the wickedness of evil men though it be veiled with religion, and shall not merely see it as an idle spectator but observe it as a judge to punish it. Keil and Delitzsch, rendering the neighbouring lines, keep the stress on knowledge that issues in reckoning. So the debate is real if narrow: whether the closing words affirm that God will surely consider and requite the sin he sees, or concede that for now he seems to take no notice — a difference that touches the whole problem of the book, and that Zophar, pressing only the certainty of judgment, never feels.
12:
The hardest verse of the speech follows, a proverb whose very grammar the witnesses cannot fully untangle: "for vain man would be wise, though man be born like a wild ass's colt." The reformed John Gill reads "hollow" or empty man — void of all good, yet who "would be wise," that is, would be thought so, valuing himself on a wisdom he will not submit to; though he allows the word may mean rather that such a man may be made wise, taught in the school of affliction, and notes that some render it "bold" or "audacious," of man lifting himself against God. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the traditional reading its fullest voice: man is a vain creature, empty; a foolish creature, become like the beasts that perish; a wilful, ungovernable creature, born like the wild ass's colt that regards no driver, as ch. 39:5 pictures it; and withal a proud creature that "would be wise," reaching after forbidden wisdom and, like his first parents, losing the tree of life for the tree of knowledge.

But the grammatical-historical and wesleyan-arminian witnesses confess the text a genuine crux. Keil and Delitzsch reject Gesenius's privative "man is empty and void of understanding" as contrary to the accents, and hold that the two key words are correlative — the one meaning "empty, hollow," the other "to acquire heart or marrow" — so that heart fills up the hollow space. Charles Ellicott owns the line "extremely difficult," hard even to divide into subject and predicate, and lays out three ways to take it: that but for God's hidden watching the fool would be disciplined; or that, for all providence does, hollow-hearted man stays empty and every son of Adam is born a wild ass's colt; or that by the discipline the hollow man is instructed and the colt "born a man" and humanised.

Adam Clarke multiplies the renderings still further — Coverdale's "a vayne body exalteth himself," Houbigant's "a man of sense will become prudent, but he who is as the wild ass hath no heart," the Chaldee's two turns, and the Vulgate's "vain man is puffed up with pride, and supposes himself born free like the wild ass's colt" — and confesses there is no end to the conjectures. One thing Ellicott finds pretty clear: that by the wild ass's colt Zophar means Job, suggesting that if he will become something wiser and put away his secret sin he may yet know prosperity. The witnesses do not resolve the philology; they leave the verse a monument to the difficulty of the Hebrew, agreeing only that its drift is a low estimate of man's untaught nature, and that its edge, whatever its exact words, is turned against the man on the ash-heap.
13:
With the doctrine of God's greatness laid down, Zophar turns preacher and offers terms of recovery: "if thou prepare thine heart, and stretch out thine hands toward him." The reformed John Gill reads it as counsel to pray, but to pray aright — with a heart prepared for such service, and hands stretched out toward the God whose immensity and sovereignty he has been describing. The gesture of the outstretched hands, Gill notes, is used for the whole of religious worship and especially for prayer; and this was what all the friends pressed on Job, to humble himself and seek forgiveness. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley puts it most briefly: prepare the heart "to seek God, turning thy bold contentions with God into humble supplications."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lays out the steps of the return Zophar urges, the same counsel Eliphaz had given at ch. 5:8 and Bildad at ch. 8:5. First a man must look within and get the heart changed — the heart that wandered reduced, that was defiled cleansed, that was unfixed settled and established, for there the work of conversion must begin. Then he must look up and stretch out his hands, stirring himself to take hold on God, praying with earnestness and importunity; to give the hand to the Lord, as at 2 Chron. 30:8, is to yield ourselves to him and covenant with him. Job had prayed already, Henry grants, but Zophar would have him pray in a better manner, not as an appellant but as a humble suppliant.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets the same advice against the grain of Zophar's assumption. He bids Job make use of the powers God has given him and stretch out his hands in fervent supplication; and he draws in the sentiment of Prov. 16:1 — "to man are the preparations of the heart, but from the LORD is the answer of the tongue" — that it is man's duty to pray and God's prerogative to answer. Yet Clarke will not let the reader forget the premise beneath the kindness: "Zophar, like all the rest, is true to his principle. Job must be a wicked man, else he had not been afflicted." The counsel is sound, the witnesses agree; it is the diagnosis behind it — that some iniquity must be hid in Job's hand and some wickedness sheltered in his house — that poisons it, as the next verse will make plain.
14:
The condition is now made specific: "if iniquity be in thine hand, put it far away, and let not wickedness dwell in thy tabernacles." The reformed John Gill fastens on the words with care. As the heart must be prepared before the hands are stretched out, so it is not any hand that may be lifted to God, but a holy one — not hands full of blood or defiled with sin. And he marks a nicety of the phrasing: it is not said "if iniquity be in thine heart," but in thine hand, pointing to sin acted out and to gains ill gotten, the very things Zophar suspected in Job.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lays out the two-fold reform the verse demands. First, a man must amend what is amiss in his own conversation, or his prayers will be ineffectual: "if there be any sin which thou dost yet live in the practice of, put it far away, forsake it with detestation, stedfastly resolving never to return to it." If any of the gains of iniquity, any goods gotten by fraud or oppression, be in his hand, he must make restitution, as Zacchaeus did at Luke 19:8, and shake his hands from holding them — "the guilt of sin is not removed if the gain of sin be not restored." Second, he must do his utmost to reform his family, for the last clause bids him not suffer wickedness to dwell in his tents; Henry suspects Zophar imagined Job's great household ill-governed, and the ruin of it the punishment of its sin.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, rendering the verse and those that follow, set it as the hinge of the whole appeal: put away the evil, and the grief that has been surmounted will leave no trace, "like water that flows by." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke had already named the assumption that governs the counsel — that there must be "some iniquity in his hand, and some wickedness tolerated in his family," else he had not been afflicted. So the witnesses do not divide over the wholesomeness of the exhortation, which any penitent might heed; they divide only over its aim. Read in itself, it is a call to forsake sin and cleanse the house; read as Zophar means it, of Job, it is a charge of hidden guilt that the reader, and God, know to be false.
15:
"For then shalt thou lift up thy face without spot; yea, thou shalt be stedfast, and shalt not fear" — and the witnesses hear in the promise a genuine gospel, however wrongly Zophar applies it. The reformed John Gill reads the lifted face two ways: before men, of one walking in a good conscience, able to say with Samuel, "whose ox have I taken?"; and, better, before God, using a holy boldness and humble confidence at the throne of grace. Even the believer who is not without spot in himself, Gill adds, being washed in the blood of Christ and clothed in his righteousness, is made all fair, and may stand before God unblamable and unreproved.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps the three notes of the verse distinct: to lift up the face denotes cheerfulness and holy boldness; "without spot" is to have a clear and unspotted conscience; and to be "stedfast" is to have a strong and comfortable assurance of God's favour. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers these into the great truth that "the work of righteousness will be peace, and the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever," as Isa. 32:17 promises. Those who sincerely turn to God may expect a holy confidence toward him: they may come boldly to the throne of grace, not with the terror and amazement Job had voiced at ch. 9:34; for if our hearts condemn us not, as 1 John 3:21 says, we have confidence in our approaches to God.

Henry presses the inward side of the promise as well: those who turn to God shall have a holy composedness in themselves — "stedfast, and shalt not fear," not afraid of evil tidings, the heart being fixed. Job was now full of confusion, looking on God as his enemy and quarrelling with him; but let him submit and humble himself, Zophar urges, and his mind would be composed and freed from those frightful apprehensions of God that had put him into such agitation. The witnesses do not divide over the doctrine, which they receive as sound and even precious: a cleansed conscience gives boldness before God and quietness within. Their reserve is only that Zophar dangles it before Job as bribe and threat at once — hinting, as Henry says, that unless God speedily made such a change the friends would be confirmed in reckoning him a hypocrite — so that a true promise is bent into a false insinuation.
16:
The promised peace reaches even backward over the sufferer's past: "because thou shalt forget thy misery, and remember it as waters that pass away." The reformed John Gill reads it of former afflictions swallowed up in an abundance of later prosperity, so that in time the old distresses are forgotten — as Joseph forgot his, naming his firstborn Manasseh; and as the convinced and converted soul, filled with the love of God and the hope of eternal life, forgets its spiritual poverty and remembers its misery no more, unless it be to magnify the riches of grace.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses seize the vivid image of the passing waters. Adam Clarke pictures a rest so long and complete that Job shall scarcely remember his labour; the sufferings shall be to him like the mountain floods, which sweep everything before them — houses, tents, cattle, the produce of the field — and are then swiftly drunk up by the sandy plains over which they run: wasting and ruinous for the time, but soon over and gone. John Wesley keeps the same figure in a phrase: thou shalt remember thy misery "no more than men remember a land-flood, which as it comes, so it goes away suddenly."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry deepens the picture with a tenderer comparison. Thou shalt forget thy misery, he says, "as the mother forgets her travailing pains, for joy that the child is born," and shalt remember it as waters poured out of a vessel, which leave no taste or tincture behind them; the wounds of the present affliction shall be perfectly healed, not only without a remaining scar but without a remaining pain. Job had tried to forget his complaint and could not, his soul still having in remembrance the wormwood and the gall; here Zophar puts him in the way of it — by faith and prayer to bring his griefs and cares to God and leave them with him, and then he shall forget them. And Henry draws the abiding lesson from beneath Zophar's misapplication: "where sin sits heavily, affliction sits lightly." If we duly remember our sins, we shall in comparison with them forget our misery, much more if we obtain the comfort of a sealed pardon and a settled peace; and he whose iniquity is forgiven shall, like the healed man of Isa. 33:24, no longer say that he is sick, but forget his sickness. The witnesses do not divide; they hold up together a mercy that heals memory itself, even while they know the healing is offered to Job on terms that slander him.
17:
The picture of restored life brightens to its noon: "and thine age shall be clearer than the noonday; thou shalt shine forth, thou shalt be as the morning." The reformed John Gill takes "thine age" as the remainder of Job's days, the latter part of his life no longer clouded with adversity but lit by a prosperity outshining the sun at noon. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same unclouded prospect and admires the figure: the rest of his life shall be as the sun in the firmament giving light and heat to all around, and "thou shalt be as the morning," the sun of his prosperity rising and shining more and more unto the perfect day — an image, Clarke says, correct and elegant. John Wesley adds only that light in Scripture commonly signifies prosperity and glory, and that Job's comfort, like the morning light, shall shine brighter and brighter.

But over the words "thou shalt shine forth" the grammatical-historical witnesses find a real crux. Charles Ellicott renders the whole afresh — "there shall arise for thee a lifetime brighter than the noonday; thou shalt soar on high; thou shalt be like the morning" — the morning being conceived, as at Ps. 139:9, as having wings, and recalling the winged Sun of Righteousness of Mal. 4:2. Yet he owns that the disputed word is taken by many not as a verb of shining but as a substantive meaning "darkness," in which case the line must run, "though there be darkness, thou shalt be as the morning." Keil and Delitzsch adopt just that reading, rendering, "and thy path of life shall be brighter than mid-day; if it be dark, it shall become as morning."

So the verse is read two ways that yet meet in one hope. On the first, Job shall himself shine forth and soar like the winged dawn; on the second, even his darkness shall break into morning. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, without pressing the philology, gathers both into his exposition: though now Job's light is eclipsed it shall shine out again and more brightly than ever, his very setting sun outshining his noonday, his evening fair and clear as the morning, and his light breaking out of obscurity even in old age. The witnesses divide honestly over whether the key word means "shine" or "darkness," but not over the promise it carries: that for the man who turns to God the worst gloom is only the threshold of a brighter day. Their single reserve is the old one — that the brightness is dangled before Job as the reward of a repentance his affliction does not require.
18:
Security by day and rest by night are promised next: "and thou shalt be secure, because there is hope; yea, thou shalt dig about thee, and thou shalt take thy rest in safety." The reformed John Gill reads "secure" as safe from every returning evil, and would render it also "confident," of a soul with strong faith and full assurance in the love of God and in the promises that respect this life and the next. But over the phrase "thou shalt dig about thee" the witnesses genuinely differ. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes it neither of digging a grave nor of anxious searching, but of the eastern custom of digging for water where the tents were pitched: good wells were a prize, often stopped up or seized, as the Philistines stopped Isaac's at Gen. 26:15; in his coming prosperity Job shall dig and find living water and none shall contend with him, resting in safety while neighbouring chiefs court his friendship, a peace Clarke ties to the covenant with the stones of the field at ch. 5:23.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets aside the digging altogether: the word means rather "thou shalt look around, or search about thee," and see that thou canst lie down in safety; the same root can mean to dig and to blush, but both, he says, are incongruous and inadmissible here. John Wesley keeps the literal digging but spreads its sense — to fix the tents, which the Arabians shifted from place to place, or to plough the ground as Job's servants had at ch. 1:14, or to make a fence about his dwelling — while grounding the security, as Gill does, in a firm and well-founded confidence in God.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the theology out of the two clauses. Those who have a good hope through grace are safe, however difficult the times: "thou shalt be secure, because there is hope," for hope is an anchor of the soul, as Heb. 6:19 has it. To "dig about thee" is to be as safe as an army within its entrenchments; those who submit to God's government are taken under his protection and are safe both day and night — safe abroad at their work, no longer set upon by the plunderers who fell on Job's servants at the plough, for "the way of duty is the way of safety." The witnesses do not divide over the promised peace; they divide only over the single verb — whether Job shall dig for water and entrenchment, or look around and find himself secure — and all of them ground the rest, by day and night alike, in the hope that God gives.
19:
"Also thou shalt lie down, and none shall make thee afraid; yea, many shall make suit unto thee" — the promise of undisturbed rest crowned by the return of respect, and the witnesses dwell on both halves. The reformed John Gill pictures the first: Job shall lie down, whether on his bed or out by his flocks where they rest, and none shall disturb him or them — not thieves and robbers such as the Chaldeans and Sabeans had been to him, nor the lions and bears and wolves that prey on the fold. It is the very opposite of the life he now leads, in which every night is broken and every possession exposed; the man who was stripped and terrified shall lie down and sleep in peace.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the vivid idiom of the second clause. "Many shall make suit unto thee" is, more literally, "and many shall caress thy cheeks" — the gesture of those who court a man's favour and stroke his face in entreaty. The stereotyped English "make suit" thus hides a warmer picture: not merely petitioners at a distance, but suppliants pressing close to win the goodwill of one newly risen in the world.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry expounds both promises with a pastor's relish. To lie down and none make afraid is the reward of those who return to God as their rest: not forced to wander with no place to lay the head, nor to watch and sit up in dread of assault, but able to go to bed at bedtime, so that none shall hurt them and none so much as give them an alarm. It is a great mercy, Henry says, to have quiet nights and undisturbed sleeps, and the way to it is to keep ourselves in the love of God. As for the courting of many, he reads Zophar's shrewd forecast: suit is made to those who are eminently wise or rich or powerful, and Zophar knew Job well enough to foresee that, however low the present ebb, once the tide turned it would flow as high as ever, and the man now slighted would again be the darling of his country — the foolish at last coming to the wise, as the foolish virgins came begging oil. The witnesses do not divide; together they set the quiet of undisturbed sleep beside the honour of a courted friendship, the two faces of the peace Zophar holds out.
20:
The speech ends where all such speeches end, in the dark lot of the wicked: "but the eyes of the wicked shall fail, and they shall not escape, and their hope shall be as the giving up of the ghost." The reformed John Gill reads the failing eyes either of grief and envy at another's prosperity or, more likely, of a vain looking for good things and deliverance that never come. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws it out: the wicked shall be continually looking for help and rescue, but their expectation shall be cut off, for "escape perishes from them," flight from the impending destruction being impossible; and their hope shall be but "an exhalation of breath," a mere wish of the mind, so that they give up their hope and their ghost together. John Wesley reads the same three strokes — eyes failing with grief or with long looking for what they shall never attain, hope that never obtains deliverance but perishes, a hope as vain and desperate as the hope of life in a man at the very point of death.

Over the last clause the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets a small correction: "omit the as of comparison" — the wicked man's hope is not merely like a dying breath, it is the very breathing out of the soul, expiring as he expires. With that he marks the close of the whole: "thus ends the first part of this mighty argument," the first movement of the grand poem, as the three friends' opening round of speeches comes to its end.

The witnesses do not divide over the dark verse, but Clarke will not let Zophar leave the stage unjudged. His premises, Clarke grants, were in general good and his conclusions legitimate; "but his application of them to Job's case was totally erroneous," proceeding still on the assumption that Job was a wicked man whom affliction was unmasking. The failing eyes and expiring hope Zophar hangs over Job as a threat belong, in truth, to a wickedness that is not his; the doom is real, but the man is misjudged. Clarke notes too that Zophar seems to reckon all rewards and punishments distributed in this life, his knowledge scarcely reaching beyond the grave — and gives thanks for the clearer light since granted, "God grant that we may make a good use of it." So the first cycle of the friends closes: their doctrine of God's greatness and man's vanity often true and weighty, as Prov. 11:7 would confirm of the wicked's perishing hope, yet every stroke of it aimed, by the men who wield it, at the one sufferer it does not fit.
